author: Fuzzypet
quote:
Thirteen years. That's how long we waited for another mainline Grand Theft Auto, and the result is deeply disappointing. GTA VI looks spectacular, but its enormous map and staggering budget cannot disguise its shortcomings. I expected Rockstar to advance the franchise, not prove that technological ambition and great game design are two different things.

Start with performance. Every launch console, including PS5 Pro, is capped at 30 FPS without a 60 FPS option. In 2026, that's a major compromise for a flagship action game. Worse, even 30 FPS isn't guaranteed. Digital Foundry found drops during ordinary driving on base PS5 and sustained slowdowns in demanding combat. Xbox Series S fares worse, frequently falling into the mid-20s during driving and firefights, occasionally approaching 20 FPS under heavy stress. PS5 Pro is far more stable, but holding a 30 FPS ceiling does not make that ceiling impressive. Why must responsive gameplay be sacrificed for visual spectacle?

Then there are the bugs. Launch reports document characters falling through the map, clipping through scenery, erratic vehicle behavior, missing textures and progress-blocking glitches. Some PS5 owners have encountered repeated crashes, including during the opening. These problems aren't necessarily universal, but they are real reports. A release this anticipated should be far more reliable.

Even favorable reviews mention awkward context-sensitive controls that trigger unintended actions or make ordinary interactions frustrating. Looting, reloading and manipulating objects should not require fighting the interface. Rockstar's animations may be beautiful, but a realistic-looking character doing the wrong thing is not good design.

Combat doesn't feel like the revolution I expected, either. Beneath the visual effects, the familiar cover-and-shoot formula remains, and reviewers have criticized enemies that are too easily picked off or rarely flank intelligently. Bigger explosions are no substitute for more engaging firefights. That is a modest return after thirteen years.

The campaign is inconsistent. Reviewers describe slow stretches, storylines that outstay their welcome and some missions that feel like glorified driving assignments or rigid cinematic sequences. Yes, other missions offer more freedom than earlier GTA games, which makes the restrictions even more irritating. Why construct an elaborate sandbox if portions of the main story still insist on tightly directing the experience? I want to play Grand Theft Auto, not just watch an expensive movie.

The obsession with realism creates additional friction. Weapon carrying is restricted, with extra firearms kept in vehicles or lockers. That might increase immersion, but it can also get in the way of the chaotic experimentation GTA is known for. There is no complete first-person mode at launch, either, despite later editions of GTA V having one. Not every realistic mechanic makes a game more enjoyable, and losing a familiar option certainly isn't progress.

The map is extraordinary, but size isn't substance. More streets, interiors and crowds cannot compensate for frustrating controls or uneven missions. GTA became legendary because its worlds were entertaining playgrounds, not because their surfaces were photorealistic. I want memorable gameplay and freedom, not endless opportunities to admire reflections.

The writing isn't beyond criticism. Reviews note uneven pacing, overlong plot threads and satire that can feel stale. GTA's rebellious humor and distinct personality were central to its identity. Making everything more cinematic doesn't automatically make it more entertaining.

PC players were also excluded from the November 19 launch, with no confirmed PC release date. After thirteen years, a huge part of the fanbase is still being asked to wait.

Most baffling is the wall of 10/10 reviews. A game can be visually groundbreaking and still deserve serious criticism for its 30 FPS cap, verified performance dips, reported crashes, awkward controls and uneven pacing. Would a smaller studio receive the same forgiveness? A perfect score should demand more.

I'm not saying nobody can enjoy GTA VI. But longtime fans have every right to question its priorities. GTA IV and GTA V had flaws, yet they had distinctive personalities built around freedom and memorable chaos. After this wait, I wanted Rockstar to refine those strengths rather than become consumed by scale, realism and cinematic spectacle.

Bugs may be fixed and performance may improve. But putting presentation ahead of enjoyable play is a deeper problem. GTA VI is an astonishing visual achievement, yet for me a deeply frustrating sequel. After thirteen years, graphics and map size simply aren't enough. It feels like Rockstar remembered how to build a world but forgot what made that world fun to play in. A famous logo should never make a game immune to criticism.
